name: quantum-multi-omic-classifier
title: Quantum Multi-Omic Classifier — Genotype-to-Phenotype Mapping via Data Re-Uploading
description: This investigation evaluates the GenotypeToPhenotypeProcess — an M-qubit data-reuploading quantum classifier where each qubit encodes one omic modality (genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics). A CNOT chain entangles all modality qubits, enabling the circuit to learn cross-modality interactions natively. Performance is benchmarked against Random Forest and Logistic Regression on synthetic and (eventually) real v2ecoli zarr data.
lead: Modern biology faces a fundamental integration problem: how do variations across multiple molecular layers (genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics) combine to determine phenotype? Classical ML approaches struggle with the high dimensionality and nonlinear cross-modality interactions inherent in multi-omic data. This investigation builds and evaluates a multi-qubit quantum classifier where each omic modality maps to a dedicated qubit, and entanglement directly encodes biological cross-talk — a natural fit for the problem structure.

at_a_glance.role: Establish baseline accuracy with Random Forest and Logistic Regression
Train and evaluate the GenotypeToPhenotypeProcess on synthetic multi-omic data
Validate on real v2ecoli zarr stores once available

how_to_read: Start with the synthetic data evaluation (study 2) to understand the quantum classifier's behavior. Compare with study 1 (classical baselines). Study 3 only applies once real v2ecoli data is available. The Marimo notebook (demo/gt2p_quantum_classifier.py) provides an interactive walkthrough.
biological_story: The central dogma of molecular biology describes information flow from DNA → RNA → Protein → Metabolite → Phenotype. Each step is a nonlinear transformation affected by the previous layer's state. In our quantum classifier, each modality gets its own qubit: genomics on qubit 0, transcriptomics on qubit 1, etc. Feature encoding via Rot gates maps measured values into quantum rotations. A CNOT chain entangles adjacent modality qubits (0↔1, 1↔2, 2↔3), mirroring the sequential cross-talk of the central dogma. After training, the entanglement strength between qubit pairs reflects learned biological interaction strength.
question: Can a multi-qubit, cross-modality entangled quantum classifier outperform classical ML baselines in predicting binary phenotypes from synthetic multi-omic data?
hypothesis: The entanglement-based architecture will capture cross-modality interactions more effectively than classical methods, yielding higher AUC-ROC on held-out test sets, especially when nonlinear interactions between modalities drive phenotype.

acceptance_criteria.behavior: Quantum classifier AUC-ROC is within 0.05 of the Random Forest baseline AUC-ROC.
ZarrMultiOmicLoader returns non-None for at least 3 modality paths from a real v2ecoli zarr store.

executive.what_is_this: An investigation into whether a purpose-built multi-qubit quantum classifier can improve phenotype prediction from multi-omic data by using entanglement to model biological cross-talk between molecular layers.
executive.verdict: Not yet run — synthetic benchmarks planned.
decisions_needed: Which classical baselines to include (RF, LR, XGBoost, SVM)?
What is the minimum acceptable AUC-ROC for claiming quantum advantage?
Should evaluation use cross-validation or fixed train/test split?

scientific_argument.main_claim: Multi-qubit entanglement-based classifiers can match or exceed classical methods on multi-omic integration tasks with strong cross-modality interactions.
evidence_for: CNOT chain directly models pairwise modality interactions
Quantum fidelity provides a continuous similarity score
One qubit per modality preserves biological interpretability
evidence_against: Synthetic data may favor quantum circuits over classical methods
Current simulation-only — no real hardware validation
Small feature spaces may not expose quantum advantage
caveats: All results are from classical simulation of quantum circuits
Synthetic data uses a known generative model that may bias results
Real multi-omic validation (v2ecoli zarr) is not yet available
